extensions: Add a per-platform rate limiter enforced at the dispatch layer — Twitter/X, LinkedIn, and Instagram all have per-user posting quotas, and a user who hits multiple milestones in quick succession will trigger silent API rejections without this guard. Track post timestamps per (user_id, platform) in Redis with a sliding window.

Build milestone event emission as a named event on an internal event bus rather than calling the social post function inline. This decouples the posting pipeline from milestone detection, making it independently deployable and extensible to future consumers (push notifications, email, analytics) without touching milestone code.

Add a dead-letter queue for failed post attempts with structured retry: transient failures retry with exponential backoff up to 3 attempts; permanent failures (invalid token, account suspended, platform policy rejection) flag the user's connected account as needing reauthorisation.
nonObviousAngles: Posting on a user's behalf without a confirmation step likely violates the Terms of Service of every major social platform. Twitter/X Developer Agreement, LinkedIn API Terms, and Meta's Platform Policy all require automated posts be clearly disclosed and that users retain meaningful control. This is a disqualifying violation that can result in app-level API access revocation — killing the entire social integration feature, not just this variant.

Storing long-lived write-capable OAuth tokens server-side creates a high-value credential store that is a named attack target. If the token store is breached, an attacker can post arbitrary content to every connected user account simultaneously. The security architecture (encryption at rest, token rotation, scope minimisation) must be designed before any write-capable OAuth integration ships.

weaknesses.text: The assumption that users have explicitly consented to automated posting in a way that satisfies platform ToS disclosure requirements is unverified and almost certainly false. OAuth scopes grant technical write access; they do not constitute informed consent to automated, no-preview posting. GDPR Article 6, CCPA, and every major platform ToS require distinct, specific consent for automated content publication. Shipping without an explicit, auditable per-user consent gate is a legal exposure, not a configuration gap.
weaknesses.label: blocking

weaknesses.text: Server-side OAuth token storage is described but no security model is specified. Refresh tokens for write-scope social accounts are high-value credentials — a platform breach, misconfigured storage, or compromised internal service account gives an attacker the ability to post to every connected user account simultaneously. At any meaningful user scale, a token leak becomes a mass-posting incident that permanently destroys user trust and violates platform developer policies, resulting in app-level bans.
weaknesses.label: blocking

weaknesses.text: The 'no preview or confirmation step' design, combined with dead-letter queue retry logic, creates a scenario where a post attempt fails transiently and retries hours later — after the user has decided they do not want it published. There is no cancellation window, no in-flight post revocation, and no mechanism for a user to say 'do not retry this one.' The retry queue becomes an uncontrollable deferred posting system with no user-facing control surface.
weaknesses.label: blocking

weaknesses.text: The Redis rate limiter tracks post timestamps per (user_id, platform) but does not address what happens when multiple milestones are triggered faster than the rate limit window allows. Excess posts are either silently dropped or queued indefinitely — silent drops mean milestones are completed but posts never publish, and indefinite queueing means stale posts fire hours later, context-free.
weaknesses.label: resolvable

weaknesses.text: Post content (copy, formatting, media) is specified as 'pre-defined or programmatic' but neither path is scoped. Pre-defined copy for 10+ milestones across 3+ platforms with platform-specific character limits requires a content management system. Programmatic generation implies an LLM or template engine. This is hidden scope doubling — the dispatch pipeline cannot be built without the content layer decided first.
weaknesses.label: resolvable

risks: Platform developer policy violation: Twitter/X, LinkedIn, and Meta prohibit automated posting without clear user disclosure and control. Violation can result in app-level bans — every connected user loses social integration permanently.

Mass-posting incident at launch: if a milestone event is emitted incorrectly (duplicate event, event bus replay after a deployment), every user who has reached that milestone gets posted simultaneously — platform spam detection flags the OAuth application, triggering a platform-wide ban before engineering can respond.

Permission revocation not handled: a user who revokes OAuth access on the platform side will have their token silently invalidated. The dead-letter queue will retry against an invalid token with no user-facing notification or re-consent flow.

Audit trail gap: there is no specified log of what was posted, when, on whose behalf, and with what content. A GDPR Subject Access Request ('what did you post on my behalf?') cannot be answered without this.
failureModes: Event bus replay after a bad deployment causes every milestone event from the past 24 hours to re-emit. The dispatch pipeline treats these as new events, posts duplicates to every affected user's social accounts, platform spam detection kills the OAuth application, and posts on external platforms cannot be retracted programmatically at scale.

A post fires immediately to LinkedIn containing a formatting bug (unclosed template variable, null milestone name rendered as 'null'). The broken post is live on the user's professional profile before any engineer is alerted, with no confirmation step as a human review gate.

An internal service breach exposes the OAuth token store. The attacker uses stored tokens to post arbitrary content to connected user accounts. Because the post-dispatch pipeline already has a working code path for posting as any user, no additional authentication barrier exists between 'dispatch service can post' and 'any internal caller can trigger a post as any user.'

userChallenges: The 'no preview or confirmation step' assumption conflicts directly with how users understand social media posting. Users treat their social profiles as curated self-presentation. Consent at OAuth connection time is not the same as consent to any specific post content. When a user shares an embarrassing milestone or a post goes out at a professionally inappropriate moment, they will blame the product and revoke access — not themselves for connecting the account.

Generic milestone posts are socially inauthentic. Users on social media are acutely sensitive to bot-generated or marketing filler content. A post saying 'I just hit Level 10 in [App Name]!' without the user's voice attached will be flagged by their followers as spam, or embarrass the user in front of a professional network. The zero-confirmation design means the user has no opportunity to add personal context, adjust tone, or suppress a milestone they would not choose to publicise.

The dead-letter queue introduces a silent failure mode users will not detect. If a post fails and lands in the queue, the user believes it went out, their followers see nothing, and the retry may fire at an arbitrary later time — after the moment has passed or in a context that no longer makes sense. The user discovers the failure only when a colleague mentions they never saw the post.
adoptionRisks: Users who have been burned by any auto-posting product will refuse to connect social accounts at all once they learn posts go out without confirmation. The feature requires OAuth connection to work, but the 'no confirmation' design is exactly what causes users to decline or immediately revoke that connection. The feature cannibalises its own prerequisite.

The existing workaround is manual sharing, which users already do when they want to share a milestone. Manual sharing lets the user choose the platform, write their own caption, pick the timing, and decide whether this milestone is worth sharing. The auto-post feature does not remove a painful step — it removes control the user actively values.

The per-platform rate limiter creates an invisible throttle users will not understand. If a user hits three milestones in one session and only one post goes out, they will assume the system is broken or other milestones 'didn't count.' There is no user-facing explanation for why some milestones posted and others did not.

The OAuth scope requirement ('write scope stored server-side') is a trust barrier increasingly hard to clear. Following high-profile data breaches and social media API abuse scandals, users are more reluctant than ever to grant write access to third-party apps. App store consent screens display 'this app can post on your behalf' explicitly, causing significant drop-off in OAuth completion rates.

strengths: The event bus architecture (Builder extension 2) is the right decoupling pattern — it enables future channels (push, email, analytics) without touching milestone code and makes the posting pipeline independently deployable.
The dead-letter queue with structured retry policy (Builder extension 3) is correct infrastructure for any async external API integration — the pattern is reusable beyond social posting.
The rate limiter per (user_id, platform) in Redis is the right data model and scope — it prevents API quota violations that would otherwise be invisible and unrecoverable.
suggestedPivots: Add a confirmation step: a short hold queue (60 seconds) between milestone detection and post dispatch, surfaced as an in-app notification with a 'post now / edit / skip' prompt — this satisfies platform ToS human-in-the-loop requirements while preserving low friction.
Commission legal review of the consent mechanism against GDPR, CCPA, and each target platform's developer policy before any OAuth write-scope integration ships.
Scope the MVP to a single platform and 2–3 milestone types with hardcoded, manually reviewed copy — defer multi-platform formatting and content templating to a separate sprint.
openQuestions: Has LinkedIn Partner Programme approval and Meta App Review been applied for? Both require advance platform approval for automated posting, and review timelines are 4–8 weeks.
Does the existing OAuth integration request write scope, or only read scope? If read-only, the OAuth flow must be re-designed and existing users must re-authorise.

What is the actual share-to-post conversion rate when users are shown a preview step versus no preview — is there evidence that removing the confirmation step increases net shares, or only posts-sent while decreasing user satisfaction?
